title: Freelance Kill Fee and Cancellation Kit
description: Know what you're owed when a client cancels mid-project. Four plain-English cancellation clauses (simple, staged, by notice, retainer) with pause and silence rules, a line-by-line kill fee worksheet, 10 ready-to-send emails from cancellation to final reminder, a handover checklist that ties files to payment, a full worked example of a $6,400 website stopped in week 4, and a cancellation log.

files.README.md:
# Freelance Kill Fee and Cancellation Kit

The client emails: "We've decided not to go ahead." You're four weeks into
an eight-week project. You turned down other work to keep the time free.
What are you owed, how do you ask for it, and what do you hand over?

This kit answers those questions before they happen, by putting a clear
cancellation clause in every contract, and after they happen, with a
worksheet that turns "what's fair?" into a number and emails that ask for
it without burning the relationship.

## What's inside

| File | What it's for | Time needed |
|---|---|---|
| cancellation-clauses.md | Four plain-English cancellation clauses to adapt for your contracts, with notes on when to use each | 20 min, once |
| kill-fee-worksheet.md | Work out exactly what to invoice when a project is cancelled, line by line | 15 min per cancellation |
| cancellation-emails.md | 10 ready-to-send emails: client cancels, client "pauses", client goes silent, no clause in the contract, and when you need to step away | Copy as needed |
| handover-checklist.md | What to deliver, what to hold until paid, and how to close the project cleanly | 10 min per cancellation |
| worked-example.md | A full cancellation from first email to paid invoice: a $6,400 website stopped in week 4 | 5 min read |
| cancellation-log.csv | Track cancellations, what you invoiced and what you collected | 2 min each |

## How to use it

**Before your next contract (do this once)**

1. Read `cancellation-clauses.md` and pick the clause that fits how you
   work. Most project freelancers should start with Clause B (staged).
2. Fill in the brackets and add it to your contract or terms.
3. Mention it in one line in your proposal, so it's never a surprise.

**When a client cancels or pauses**

1. Don't reply in the first hour. Open `kill-fee-worksheet.md`.
2. Fill in the worksheet. It gives you the number your clause allows and a
   fair number if you have no clause.
3. Pick the matching email from `cancellation-emails.md` and send it with
   the invoice.
4. Work through `handover-checklist.md`. Release final files when the
   invoice is paid.
5. Log it in `cancellation-log.csv` (delete the example rows first).

## Four principles

1. **Cancellation is normal, not personal.** Budgets get cut, people leave,
   priorities change. A calm, prepared reply makes it much more likely the
   client comes back when things settle.
2. **Agree the rules before the work starts.** A kill fee that's in the
   contract is a formality. A kill fee you invent after cancellation is a
   negotiation.
3. **Charge for what you did and what you lost, not for revenge.** Work
   completed, costs you can't get back, and a reasonable share of the time
   you reserved. That's easy to defend.
4. **Tie the handover to payment.** Clients get the work they paid for.
   That's fair to both sides and it is your best collection tool.

## Who it's for

Designers, developers, writers, marketers, video makers, consultants and
other project freelancers who book work weeks ahead and lose real money
when a project stops halfway.

## A note on contracts

This kit is general information, not legal advice. Contract rules differ
by country and state, and some consumer-protection laws limit what you can
charge individuals (as opposed to businesses). If a cancellation involves a
large amount, or you sell to consumers, have a local lawyer review your
clause once. It is usually a short, inexpensive job.

## Making it yours

Everything in [square brackets] is a placeholder for your details. Change
the tone of the emails to sound like you. Shorter is usually better.

## Licence

For your own freelance business. Please don't resell or share the files.
files.cancellation-clauses.md:
# Cancellation clauses you can adapt

A cancellation clause answers four questions in advance:

1. How does either side end the project? (In writing, with how much notice?)
2. What does the client pay for work already done?
3. What extra, if anything, does the client pay for the time you reserved?
4. What happens to the files and the rights to use them?

Below are four versions. Pick one, fill in the brackets, and read it out
loud. If it doesn't sound like something you'd be comfortable explaining to
a client on a call, simplify it.

> General information only, not legal advice. Laws on cancellation fees and
> consumer contracts vary. Check with a local professional if you're unsure,
> especially if your clients are individuals rather than businesses.

---

## Clause A: Simple (small projects under about $1,500)

Use when: projects are short, you take a deposit, and you want one rule
that's easy to explain.

> **Cancellation.** Either of us can cancel this project by email at any
> time. If the project is cancelled, the deposit of [50%] is non-refundable
> and covers the time reserved and work started. If work completed at the
> time of cancellation is worth more than the deposit, based on my rate of
> [$X per hour / day], I will invoice the difference. Once all invoices are
> paid, you will receive the work completed so far and the right to use it.

Why it works: the deposit already does most of the job, so there is
rarely anything to chase.

---

## Clause B: Staged (recommended for most projects)

Use when: projects run several weeks, you work in phases or milestones,
and you turn down other work to fit them in.

> **Cancellation.** Either of us may cancel this project with written
> notice by email. If the client cancels:
>
> 1. The client pays for all work completed up to the date of notice,
>    based on the milestones in this agreement, or for a milestone in
>    progress, the share of that milestone completed, at a minimum of
>    [25%] of that milestone.
> 2. The client reimburses any approved third-party costs already incurred
>    (for example stock licences, fonts, hosting or printing) that cannot
>    be cancelled or refunded.
> 3. The client pays a cancellation fee of [20%] of the remaining project
>    fee (the total project fee minus the value of work completed), to cover time reserved that cannot be rebooked at short
>    notice. [If notice is given more than [14] days before work begins, no
>    cancellation fee applies.]
>
> Payments already made count towards these amounts. Any balance is due
> within [14] days of the final invoice. Once paid in full, the client
> receives all completed work and the rights described in this agreement
> for that work.

How the numbers usually land:

| Remaining project fee | Cancellation fee at 20% | At 25% | At 30% |
|---|---|---|---|
| $1,000 | $200 | $250 | $300 |
| $3,000 | $600 | $750 | $900 |
| $6,000 | $1,200 | $1,500 | $1,800 |

Choosing the percentage: 15-25% is common for project work. Go higher if
your work is booked months ahead and very hard to rebook (wedding
photography, event work, large builds). Go lower if you have a waiting
list and can fill gaps quickly.

---

## Clause C: Sliding scale by notice (booked dates, events, shoots)

Use when: you reserve specific dates and the loss depends on how much
notice you get.

> **Cancellation and rescheduling.** If the client cancels:
>
> - more than [30] days before the booked start date: the deposit is
>   refunded minus [$X] for planning work already done;
> - [8-30] days before: the deposit of [30%] is non-refundable;
> - [7] days or fewer before: [50%] of the total fee is payable;
> - after work has begun: the client pays for all work completed plus
>   [50%] of the remaining fee.
>
> The client may reschedule once, free of charge, with at least [14] days'
> notice, to a date within [6 months], subject to availability.

Tip: the free reschedule option turns many cancellations into
postponements. Clients like having a way out that doesn't cost them.

---

## Clause D: Retainer or ongoing work

Use when: the client pays monthly for a set amount of your time.

> **Ending the retainer.** Either of us can end this retainer with
> [30] days' written notice. The retainer fee is payable for the notice
> period, and I will continue to deliver the agreed work during that time.
> Unused hours [do not roll over / roll over for one month only] and are
> not refundable. Work in progress at the end of the notice period will be
> delivered as it stands, or completed at my standard rate of [$X] if the
> client prefers.

---

## Add these lines to any clause

**Pauses.** Without a pause rule, "let's pause for a few weeks" can turn
into months with your calendar blocked and nothing paid.

> If the client pauses the project for more than [21] days, I may treat it
> as cancelled under this clause, or invoice for work completed to date and
> reschedule the remaining work based on my availability at the time.

**Silence.** Projects often die quietly rather than being cancelled.

> If I don't receive feedback or materials needed to continue for [30]
> days after a written reminder, the project will be treated as paused.

**Your side.** Clients trust a clause more when it's fair both ways.

> If I need to cancel for reasons within my control, I will refund any
> payment for work not yet delivered, hand over all work completed, and
> where possible recommend another professional.

---

## One line for your proposal

Add this under your price or payment terms so the clause is never a
surprise:

> "If plans change, the cancellation terms are simple: you pay for work
> done plus [20%] of what's left, and you keep everything completed so far."

## Checklist before you use your clause

- [ ] The percentage feels fair to you and you could explain it calmly
- [ ] "Written notice" includes email, so there's no argument about method
- [ ] It says what happens to deposits already paid
- [ ] It says when the final invoice is due
- [ ] It links handover and usage rights to full payment
- [ ] It covers pauses and silence, not just cancellation
- [ ] It's fair in both directions
- [ ] You've checked whether consumer-protection rules apply to your clients
files.cancellation-emails.md:
# Cancellation emails

Ten emails for the moments when a project stops. Each one is short on
purpose. Replace everything in [square brackets], read it once out loud,
and cut anything that doesn't sound like you.

General rules:

- Reply within one working day, but not within the first hour.
- Thank them and stay warm. You want to be the first person they call
  when the project comes back.
- Put the money and the next step in the same email. Two emails feel like
  two demands.
- Attach the invoice. Don't make them ask for it.

---

## 1. Client cancels, you have a clause

**Subject:** Re: [Project name] - wrapping up

> Hi [Name],
>
> Thanks for letting me know, and I completely understand. Plans change.
>
> Here's how we'll close things out, following the cancellation terms in
> our agreement:
>
> - Work completed to [date]: [milestones done, share of current one]
> - Non-refundable costs: [items], receipts attached
> - Cancellation fee: [20%] of the remaining project fee
>
> After your deposit, the balance is [$amount]. The invoice is attached
> and due by [date].
>
> Once it's paid I'll send over everything completed so far: [list the
> files]. They'll be yours to use as set out in our agreement.
>
> It's been great working on this with you. If the project comes back to
> life, I'd be glad to pick it up from where we stopped.
>
> [Your name]

---

## 2. Client cancels, no clause in the contract

Ask for work completed and costs. Mention reserved time as a reasonable
request, not a demand.

**Subject:** Re: [Project name] - next steps

> Hi [Name],
>
> Thanks for telling me, and sorry to hear the project won't go ahead.
>
> I've put together a final invoice for the work completed up to today:
> [milestones / hours], plus [$amount] for [licences / costs] that can't be
> refunded. Receipts are attached. The total after your deposit is
> [$amount].
>
> I'd also held [number] weeks in my calendar for the rest of the project
> and turned down other work to do it. I've added a small fee of [$amount]
> ([15%] of the remaining fee) to cover part of that time. I hope that
> feels fair. If you'd like to talk it through, I'm happy to.
>
> As soon as the invoice is settled I'll send everything completed so far.
>
> [Your name]

---

## 3. Client cancels before work begins

**Subject:** Re: [Project name] - no problem

> Hi [Name],
>
> Thanks for letting me know before we started. That's very considerate.
>
> [If no fee applies:] As we agreed, there's no cancellation fee at this
> stage. I'll refund your deposit of [$amount] by [date].
>
> [If the deposit is kept:] As set out in our agreement, the deposit
> covers the time reserved and the planning work done so far, so there's
> nothing more to pay.
>
> If the timing works better later in the year, just get in touch and
> I'll check my availability.
>
> [Your name]

---

## 4. Client says "let's pause" with no restart date

**Subject:** Re: [Project name] - pausing

> Hi [Name],
>
> No problem at all, thanks for the heads-up.
>
> To keep things simple while we're paused, I'll invoice for the work
> completed so far ([milestones / hours], [$amount]). That way nothing is
> left hanging on either side.
>
> I can't hold the rest of the dates open indefinitely, so I'll release
> them for other work. When you're ready to restart, let me know and I'll
> give you the earliest dates I have. Usually that's within [2-4] weeks.
>
> If you'd rather lock in a restart date now, I can hold it for you.
> [Optional: That would need a [$amount] booking fee, credited to the
> next invoice.]
>
> [Your name]

---

## 5. Pause has gone past your pause limit

**Subject:** [Project name] - checking in after the pause

> Hi [Name],
>
> It's been [number] weeks since we paused [project name], so I wanted to
> check in.
>
> Under our agreement, a pause of more than [21] days can be treated as a
> cancellation. I'd rather not do that if the project is still alive. Could
> you let me know by [date] which of these fits best?
>
> 1. Restart: we pick dates and carry on.
> 2. Stay paused: we close out the current phase now and restart later at
>    my availability.
> 3. Stop: I'll send the final invoice and hand over everything completed.
>
> Any of these is completely fine. I just want us both to know where
> things stand.
>
> [Your name]

---

## 6. Client has gone silent

Send after two unanswered reminders about feedback or materials.

**Subject:** [Project name] - shall we close this for now?

> Hi [Name],
>
> I haven't heard back about [the design feedback / the content] since
> [date], so I'm guessing things are busy on your side.
>
> If I don't hear from you by [date], I'll assume the project is on hold,
> send a final invoice for the work done so far ([$amount]), and release
> your dates. You'll still be very welcome to restart later.
>
> If you'd like to keep going, just reply with a quick "still on" and
> we'll pick it up.
>
> [Your name]

---

## 7. Client disputes the cancellation fee

**Subject:** Re: Final invoice for [project name]

> Hi [Name],
>
> Thanks for coming back to me on this. I understand it's not a nice
> surprise when a project stops.
>
> The fee is from section [X] of our agreement, which you can see here:
> "[quote the clause in one or two lines]". It covers part of the [number]
> weeks I'd set aside for your project and can't fill at short notice.
>
> If it helps, I'm happy to waive the [$amount] cancellation fee if the
> rest of the invoice ([$amount]) is paid by [date, about 7 days away].
>
> [Your name]

Make the trade offer only once, and only if you already decided in Step 7
of the worksheet that you'd accept it.

---

## 8. Final invoice reminder

**Subject:** Reminder: [project name] final invoice, due [date]

> Hi [Name],
>
> A quick reminder that the final invoice for [project name] ([$amount])
> was due on [date]. I've attached it again here.
>
> As soon as it's paid I'll send over the completed files. Could you let me
> know when I can expect payment?
>
> [Your name]

---

## 9. Handover email (after payment)

**Subject:** [Project name] - your files

> Hi [Name],
>
> Thanks, payment received.
>
> Here's everything completed for [project name]:
>
> - [File / folder 1]: [what it is]
> - [File / folder 2]: [what it is]
> - [Notes / passwords / documentation]: [where to find them]
>
> A few notes if someone else picks this up: [one to three helpful
> points, for example which pages are finished, what's left, any quirks].
>
> I've [removed my access / transferred ownership] of [accounts]. Please
> check everything opens correctly and let me know within [7] days if
> anything's missing.
>
> Thanks again, and good luck with [next step]. If you restart the project
> later, I'd be glad to help.
>
> [Your name]

---

## 10. You need to step away from a project

For illness, a family emergency, or a client relationship that has broken
down. Be honest, brief and generous.

**Subject:** [Project name] - an update from me

> Hi [Name],
>
> I'm sorry to say I need to step away from [project name]. [One honest
> sentence: "Because of a family matter I can't give it the time it
> needs." / "I don't think I'm the right fit for where the project is
> going."]
>
> I don't want to leave you stuck, so here's my plan:
>
> - I'll hand over all work completed so far by [date], with notes.
> - I'll invoice only for completed work ([$amount]) and refund
>   [$amount] of the deposit for work not yet done. [Or: there is nothing
>   more to pay.]
> - [Optional: I can recommend [name / type of specialist] who could take
>   it on.]
>
> I'm sorry for the disruption and grateful for the work we did together.
>
> [Your name]

files.handover-checklist.md:
# Handover checklist

Use this for every cancelled, paused or abandoned project. It protects you
(nothing released before payment) and the client (nothing missing once
they've paid).

## The rule

**Released on payment:** the final files and the right to use them.

**Released straight away, whatever happens:** anything that belongs to
the client already. Their logins, their content, their brand files, their
data, and access to their own accounts. Never hold the client's own
property as leverage. It is unfair, and in many places it can create legal
problems for you.

---

## 1. Same day as notice

- [ ] Stop work. Note the date and time you stopped.
- [ ] Save and back up everything as it stands. Don't tidy or delete yet.
- [ ] Log your final hours for the project.
- [ ] Cancel or pause anything that costs money: subcontractors, bookings,
      subscriptions, print orders. Ask for refunds where possible.
- [ ] Note which costs could not be refunded, and save the receipts.
- [ ] Fill in `kill-fee-worksheet.md`.

## 2. Within one working day

- [ ] Send the right email from `cancellation-emails.md` with the invoice.
- [ ] List exactly what the client will receive on payment (in the email).
- [ ] Release your calendar for the freed-up dates.
- [ ] Tell anyone waiting for that time (a lead you'd turned away, a
      subcontractor) that you have space.

## 3. Prepare the handover pack (while you wait for payment)

Make it the pack you'd want to receive if you were taking over the
project.

- [ ] Completed files in open, usable formats (plus source files if your
      agreement includes them).
- [ ] Work in progress, clearly labelled as unfinished.
- [ ] A short handover note: what's done, what's not, anything unusual.
- [ ] Licences and receipts for fonts, images or plugins bought for them,
      with a note of what each licence covers.
- [ ] A list of accounts, tools and services used on the project and who
      owns each one.
- [ ] Any passwords you created for the client (shared securely, never in
      a plain email).

Folder structure that works:

```
[Client] - [Project] - Handover [date]/
  01 Completed/
  02 Work in progress/
  03 Licences and receipts/
  HANDOVER NOTES.txt
```

## 4. After payment

- [ ] Send the handover pack with email 9.
- [ ] Transfer ownership of anything you set up in your name for them
      (domains, hosting, social accounts, repositories, design files).
- [ ] Remove your own access to their accounts, or ask them to remove it.
- [ ] Ask them to confirm everything opens within [7] days.
- [ ] Mark the invoice paid and fill in `cancellation-log.csv`.

## 5. If payment doesn't arrive

- [ ] Day 1 after due date: send email 8.
- [ ] Day 7: short follow-up, offer a call.
- [ ] Day 14: a firm, polite note that you'll follow the late payment
      steps in your agreement.
- [ ] Day 30: consider a formal letter or a small-claims process where
      you live. Keep every email.
- [ ] Throughout: keep the client's own property available to them.
      Only your completed work is held.

## 6. Close-out (15 minutes)

- [ ] What triggered the cancellation? Could you have spotted it earlier?
- [ ] Did your clause cover this situation? If not, update it now.
- [ ] Did you get a deposit large enough to cover the first phase?
- [ ] Is this client worth a friendly check-in in [3 months]? Put it in
      your calendar.
files.kill-fee-worksheet.md:
# Kill fee worksheet

Fill this in before you reply to a cancellation. It takes about 15 minutes
and gives you a number you can explain line by line. The right-hand column
shows the worked example from `worked-example.md` (a $6,400 website
cancelled in week 4) so you can see how each line works.

Use Part A if your contract has a cancellation clause. Use Part B if it
doesn't, or if the clause is unclear.

---

## Step 1: The facts

| Question | Your answer | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Client and project | | Harbour Physio, new website |
| Total agreed fee | | $6,400 |
| Date the client gave notice (by email) | | 12 Nov |
| Which week of the project was it? | | Week 4 of 8 |
| Does your contract have a cancellation clause? | | Yes, Clause B, 20% |
| Amount already paid | | $1,920 deposit |
| Did they cancel, pause or go silent? | | Cancelled |

If they said "pause", check your pause rule first. If there's no date to
restart, treat it as a cancellation in all but name and say so politely
(see email 4 in `cancellation-emails.md`).

---

## Step 2: Value of work completed

List every milestone or phase. For finished ones, use the full price. For
the one in progress, estimate the share done honestly. A good test: if you
handed this work to another freelancer, what share of the job would they
say was finished?

| Milestone | Price | Share done | Value | Example |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. | | | | Discovery and sitemap: $1,200 x 100% = $1,200 |
| 2. | | | | Design, 6 page templates: $2,000 x 100% = $2,000 |
| 3. | | | | Build: $2,400 x 30% = $720 |
| 4. | | | | Launch and training: $800 x 0% = $0 |
| **Work completed (W)** | | | | **$3,920** |

Hourly instead? Hours logged x your rate. Example: 34 hours x $115 =
$3,910, which agrees with the milestone figure, a good sign.

If your clause has a minimum for a milestone in progress (for example
25%), use the higher of the minimum and the real share done.

---

## Step 3: Costs you can't get back (C)

Only costs the client approved, or that were clearly part of the job, and
that you can't cancel or refund. Keep the receipts.

| Item | Amount | Can it be refunded or reused? | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| | | | Font licence for client's domain: $90, not refundable |
| | | | Stock photos licensed for client: $60, not refundable |
| | | | Subcontractor booked for week 5: $0, cancelled in time |
| **Costs (C)** | | | **$150** |

---

## Step 4: Reserved time (R)

### Part A: You have a clause

Remaining project fee = total fee - W.

Cancellation fee = remaining project fee x your clause percentage.

| Line | Your figure | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Total fee | | $6,400 |
| minus work completed (W) | | $3,920 |
| = remaining project fee | | $2,480 |
| x clause percentage | | 20% |
| **= cancellation fee (R)** | | **$496** |

Check any "no fee if notice is given more than X days before work begins"
rule. It won't apply mid-project, but it often applies to early cancellations.

### Part B: No clause

Without a clause you're asking, not invoicing, for the reserved-time part.
Many freelancers charge only W + C in this case and ask for R as a
reasonable request. Work out what you actually lost:

| Question | Your answer | Example (if no clause) |
|---|---|---|
| How many days were booked for this project from now on? | | 12 working days |
| How many of those can you realistically fill in the next 4 weeks? | | About 6 |
| Days you'll probably lose | | 6 |
| x your day rate | | $920 |
| = real loss | | $5,520 |
| Reasonable ask (often 10-25% of the remaining fee, never more than the real loss) | | $372 (15%) |

Asking for a small share of a real loss, with the reason, is usually
accepted. Asking for the whole remaining fee usually isn't, and isn't
what courts in most places would award anyway.

---

## Step 5: Total and balance

| Line | Your figure | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Work completed (W) | | $3,920 |
| + Costs (C) | | $150 |
| + Cancellation fee (R) | | $496 |
| = **Total owed** | | **$4,566** |
| - Already paid | | $1,920 |
| = **Balance to invoice** | | **$2,646** |

If the amount already paid is more than the total owed, you owe a refund
of the difference. Send it promptly. It's the right thing to do and the
client will remember it.

---

## Step 6: Sanity checks before you send

- [ ] Could you explain every line in one sentence on a call?
- [ ] Does W match your time log roughly? (If not, which is right?)
- [ ] Do you have receipts for every cost in C?
- [ ] Is R within what your clause says (or a modest ask if no clause)?
- [ ] Have you listed what the client receives when the balance is paid?
- [ ] Have you set a due date that matches your contract (for example 14 days)?

## Step 7: Decide what you'll accept

Decide now, not mid-email, what you'd settle for if the client pushes back.

| | Your figure | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Full amount | | $2,646 |
| Would accept (for example waive R if paid within 7 days) | | $2,150 |
| Won't go below (W + C minus amount paid) | | $2,150 |

Waiving the cancellation fee in exchange for fast payment is a useful,
generous-looking trade that still covers all the work you did.

## Invoice line wording

Use clear lines so nothing needs explaining:

```
Website project - work completed to 12 Nov (milestones 1-2, 30% of build)   $3,920.00
Non-refundable licences (font, stock photography) - receipts attached        $150.00
Cancellation fee per clause [X]: 20% of remaining project fee ($2,480)       $496.00
Less: deposit received 20 Oct                                              -$1,920.00
Balance due by 26 Nov                                                      $2,646.00
```

# Worked example: a $6,400 website stopped in week 4

A fictional but typical case, from cancellation email to paid invoice.

## The project

Maya is a freelance web designer. Harbour Physio, a small clinic, hired
her for a new website.

| Milestone | Price | Weeks |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Discovery and sitemap | $1,200 | 1 |
| 2. Design, 6 page templates | $2,000 | 2-3 |
| 3. Build | $2,400 | 4-6 |
| 4. Launch and training | $800 | 7-8 |
| **Total** | **$6,400** | 8 weeks |

Payment terms: 30% deposit ($1,920) on signing, then invoices at the end
of milestones 2 and 4. Her contract included Clause B from this kit with a
20% cancellation fee and a 14-day payment term.

To fit the project in, Maya had turned down a $3,000 brochure job.

## What happened

**Wednesday 12 Nov, week 4.** Design was approved the week before and the
build was about 30% done. The design invoice hadn't been sent yet. The
clinic manager emailed:

> "Hi Maya, I'm really sorry, but the partners have decided to put the
> website on hold. We're merging with another clinic next year and they
> want to wait. Can we stop where we are?"

**Maya's first instinct** was to reply straight away with "No problem!" and
work the money out later. Instead she waited an hour and opened the
worksheet.

## The worksheet

| Line | Amount | How she got it |
|---|---|---|
| Discovery (done) | $1,200 | 100% of milestone 1 |
| Design (done, approved) | $2,000 | 100% of milestone 2 |
| Build (30% done) | $720 | 30% of $2,400. Clause minimum is 25%, so 30% stands |
| **Work completed (W)** | **$3,920** | Matched her time log: 34 hours x $115 = $3,910 |
| Font licence | $90 | Approved by client, not refundable |
| Stock photos | $60 | Licensed for the clinic, not refundable |
| **Costs (C)** | **$150** | Receipts attached |
| Remaining project fee | $2,480 | $6,400 - $3,920 |
| **Cancellation fee (R)** | **$496** | 20% of $2,480 |
| **Total owed** | **$4,566** | W + C + R |
| Less deposit | -$1,920 | |
| **Balance** | **$2,646** | Due in 14 days |

Her floor, decided before she replied: $2,150 (work and costs, no fee), if
paid within a week.

She also noticed the email said "on hold", not "cancelled". Her pause
rule said pauses over 21 days could be treated as a cancellation, and a
merger next year was far beyond that. She decided to treat it as a
cancellation but make restarting easy.

## Her reply (email 1, adjusted)

> Hi Jo,
>
> Thanks for letting me know, and congratulations on the merger. That's
> big news.
>
> Since the restart is likely to be next year, the simplest thing is to
> close the project out now under the cancellation terms in our agreement,
> so nothing's left open on either side:
>
> - Discovery and design, both complete: $3,200
> - Build, about 30% complete: $720
> - Font and stock photo licences (receipts attached): $150
> - Cancellation fee, 20% of the remaining project fee: $496
>
> After your deposit of $1,920, the balance is $2,646, due by 26 Nov.
> The invoice is attached.
>
> Once it's paid I'll send you the approved designs, the sitemap, the
> partly built site files and the licences, all yours to use. If the new
> clinic wants to pick the website up again, I'd love to help, and the
> designs will give us a big head start.
>
> Best,
> Maya

## The pushback

Two days later:

> "Thanks Maya. We're fine with paying for the work, but the partners
> weren't aware of a cancellation fee. Is that negotiable?"

Maya used email 7. She quoted the clause in one line, explained it
covered the build weeks she'd kept free, and offered to waive the $496 if
the remaining $2,150 was paid by 21 Nov.

## The outcome

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| 12 Nov | Cancellation email received; worksheet done; invoice sent |
| 14 Nov | Client asks about the fee |
| 14 Nov | Maya offers to waive it for payment by 21 Nov |
| 19 Nov | $2,150 paid |
| 19 Nov | Handover pack sent with email 9; Maya removed from their hosting account |
| 20 Nov | Logged in `cancellation-log.csv`; check-in reminder set for March |

**Collected in total:** $4,070 ($1,920 deposit + $2,150) for 34 hours of
work, which is about $120 an hour, just above her normal rate, with the
licences repaid.

**Without a clause** she would probably have asked only for the work done
and might have been talked down on the 30% build estimate. **Without a
deposit** she would have been chasing the full $4,070 instead of $2,150.

## What Maya changed afterwards

1. She now invoices each milestone as soon as it's approved. The unbilled
   $2,000 design invoice made this cancellation riskier than it needed to
   be.
2. She added the one-line cancellation summary to her proposals, so the
   fee is never a surprise to whoever signs.
3. She raised her deposit to cover the whole first milestone plus part of
   the second.
